newsitem.title: SPAIN: Barcelona stock exchange says no Spain merger plan.
newsitem.headline: Barcelona stock exchange says no Spain merger plan.

text.p: There are no plans to merge Spain's four stock exchanges, although moves to coordinate them better to meet the challenges of the single currency are being studied, Juan Hortala, chairman of Barcelona's bourse authority told Reuters on Thursday.

A recent report in El Pais newspaper said that the four exchanges in Madrid, Barcelona, Bilbao and Valencia were planning to merge and introduce a new organisational structure which would follow a German-type model.

"We are not planning any merger. Each of the stock exchanges works on its own and perfectly well. What (National Stock Market Commission CNMV chairman) Juan Fernandez-Armesto has proposed is that we are better coordinated, that the cash markets work closer together and that there is a coordinating body," Hortala said.
"There are internal studies about (the coordinating body), but obviously I'm not going to make those public," he said.

"The advantage of this would be to reduce transaction costs...and we'd have an integrated system to respond to the challenge of the euro. But this would be something for the medium or long term," Hortala said.
Currently, the Society of Bourses operates and owns the trading system connecting the four exchanges and is in turn owned equally by them. The CNMV acts as national watchdog.
The exchanges act as four distinct means of entry to the continuous market, in which shares are traded on a screen-based system. Each exchange has separate open-outcry trade.
CNMV chairman Juan Fernandez Armesto has called on the four bourses to combine their strengths ahead of the launch of the single currency, a spokeswoman said.
"What the chairman has made clear is that he thinks that ahead of the challenge of the euro the four exchanges should join forces to strengthen their position amid increased competition."

Of total Spanish cash trade Madrid's bourse accounts for over 75 percent of volume in pesetas, Barcelona takes up over 10 percent, Bilbao accounts for around 13 percent and Valencia one percent, according to end-1996 data from the CNMV.
"(A merger) would make no sense because of the current (ownership) system. It's not necessary to follow a German system," Hortala added.
In Germany, the eight regional bourses and the derivatives exchaange are grouped in a central holding.
